claim: Many antibiotics target the assembly of cell wall peptidoglycan.
source: Many antibiotics target the assembly of cell wall peptidoglycan, an essential, heteropolymeric mesh that encases most bacteria.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in microbiology and pharmacology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Cell wall peptidoglycan is an essential, heteropolymeric mesh that encases most bacteria.
source: Many antibiotics target the assembly of cell wall peptidoglycan, an essential, heteropolymeric mesh that encases most bacteria.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the structure and function of peptidoglycan.

claim: In rod-shaped bacteria, cell wall elongation is spatially precise.
source: In rod-shaped bacteria, cell wall elongation is spatially precise yet relies on limited pools of lipid-linked precursors that generate and are attracted to membrane disorder.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell wall synthesis.

claim: Cell wall elongation relies on limited pools of lipid-linked precursors that generate and are attracted to membrane disorder.
source: In rod-shaped bacteria, cell wall elongation is spatially precise yet relies on limited pools of lipid-linked precursors that generate and are attracted to membrane disorder.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Precursors of peptidoglycan biosynthesis are made in plasma membrane domains that are laterally and biochemically distinct from sites of cell wall assembly in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
source: By tracking enzymes, substrates, and products of peptidoglycan biosynthesis in Mycobacterium smegmatis, we show that precursors are made in plasma membrane domains that are laterally and biochemically distinct from sites of cell wall assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including fractionation, microscopy, and biochemical assays shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Membrane partitioning likely contributes to robust, orderly peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Membrane partitioning likely contributes to robust, orderly peptidoglycan synthesis, suggesting that these domains help template peptidoglycan synthesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and represents inference from the data.

claim: Membrane domains help template peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Membrane partitioning likely contributes to robust, orderly peptidoglycan synthesis, suggesting that these domains help template peptidoglycan synthesis.
evidence: This is a suggested interpretation of the data, representing inference from experimental observations.

claim: The cell wall-organizing protein DivIVA promotes domain homeostasis.
source: The cell wall-organizing protein DivIVA and the cell wall itself promote domain homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 demonstrating effects of DivIVA depletion on membrane domains.

claim: The cell wall itself promotes domain homeostasis.
source: The cell wall-organizing protein DivIVA and the cell wall itself promote domain homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from spheroplasting experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The peptidoglycan polymer feeds back on its membrane template to maintain an environment conducive to directional synthesis.
source: These data support a model in which the peptidoglycan polymer feeds back on its membrane template to maintain an environment conducive to directional synthesis.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings, representing inference from the data.

claim: Horizontal compartmentalization of precursors may be a general feature of bacillary cell wall biogenesis.
source: Our findings are applicable to rod-shaped bacteria that are phylogenetically distant from M. smegmatis, indicating that horizontal compartmentalization of precursors may be a general feature of bacillary cell wall biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multiple bacterial species shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lipid II is made by the glycosyltransferase MurG in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: The final lipid-linked precursor for peptidoglycan synthesis, lipid II, is made by the glycosyltransferase MurG in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan biosynthesis.

claim: Lipid II is flipped to the outer leaflet by MurJ.
source: Lipid II is then flipped to the outer leaflet by MurJ where its disaccharide-pentapeptide cargo is inserted into the existing cell wall by membrane-bound transglycosylases and transpeptidases (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The disaccharide-pentapeptide cargo of lipid II is inserted into the existing cell wall by membrane-bound transglycosylases and transpeptidases.
source: Lipid II is then flipped to the outer leaflet by MurJ where its disaccharide-pentapeptide cargo is inserted into the existing cell wall by membrane-bound transglycosylases and transpeptidases (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A fluid microenvironment might stimulate the activities of MurG and MraY in Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli.
source: Early in vitro work in Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli indicated that a fluid microenvironment might stimulate the activities of MurG and the upstream, lipid I synthase MraY (Norris and Manners, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bacillus subtilis MurG localizes to regions of increased fluidity (RIFs).
source: More recent in vivo data has localized Bacillus subtilis MurG to regions of increased fluidity (RIFs, Müller et al., 2016; Strahl et al., 2014), one of three classes of membrane domains that have been described in bacteria to date.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Three classes of membrane domains have been described in bacteria.
source: More recent in vivo data has localized Bacillus subtilis MurG to regions of increased fluidity (RIFs, Müller et al., 2016; Strahl et al., 2014), one of three classes of membrane domains that have been described in bacteria to date.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on prior research.

claim: In mycobacteria, intracellular membrane domains (IMD) can be separated from the conventional plasma membrane (PM-CW) by sucrose density gradient fractionation.
source: In mycobacteria, intracellular membrane domains (IMD, formerly called PMf, Morita et al., 2005) can be separated from the conventional plasma membrane (PM-CW, for plasma membrane associated with cell wall) by sucrose density gradient fractionation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and is a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The proteome and lipidome of IMD are distinct from those of the PM-CW.
source: The proteome and lipidome of IMD are distinct from those of the PM-CW (Hayashi et al., 2016; Morita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mycobacterium smegmatis MurG is enriched in the IMD.
source: Reanalysis of our proteomics data (Hayashi et al., 2016) suggested that Mycobacterium smegmatis MurG is enriched in the IMD while sequentially acting transglycosylases and transpeptidases associate with the PM-CW.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of prior proteomics data.

claim: Transglycosylases and transpeptidases associate with the PM-CW.
source: Reanalysis of our proteomics data (Hayashi et al., 2016) suggested that Mycobacterium smegmatis MurG is enriched in the IMD while sequentially acting transglycosylases and transpeptidases associate with the PM-CW.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of prior proteomics data.

claim: PM-CW-resident proteins distribute along the perimeter of live mycobacteria.
source: While PM-CW-resident proteins distribute along the perimeter of live mycobacteria, IMD-resident proteins are enriched toward sites of polar cell elongation with additional presence along the sidewalls (Hayashi et al., 2016; Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: IMD-resident proteins are enriched toward sites of polar cell elongation with additional presence along the sidewalls.
source: While PM-CW-resident proteins distribute along the perimeter of live mycobacteria, IMD-resident proteins are enriched toward sites of polar cell elongation with additional presence along the sidewalls (Hayashi et al., 2016; Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The polar enrichment of MurG-RFP resembles that of the validated IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2 or GlfT2-GFP.
source: We also noted that the polar enrichment of MurG-RFP resembles that of the validated IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2 or GlfT2-GFP (Hayashi et al., 2016; Meniche et al., 2014), but that nascent peptidoglycan at the mycobacterial poles primarily abuts rather than colocalizes with mCherry-GlfT2 (Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on observations from prior research.

claim: Nascent peptidoglycan at the mycobacterial poles primarily abuts rather than colocalizes with mCherry-GlfT2.
source: We also noted that the polar enrichment of MurG-RFP resembles that of the validated IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2 or GlfT2-GFP (Hayashi et al., 2016; Meniche et al., 2014), but that nascent peptidoglycan at the mycobacterial poles primarily abuts rather than colocalizes with mCherry-GlfT2 (Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on observations from prior research.

claim: MurG-Dendra2 is a functional fusion protein that can rescue depletion of endogenous MurG.
source: To test this model, we first expressed a functional MurG-Dendra2 fusion in M. smegmatis (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2) and assayed its distribution in membrane fractions that had been separated by a sucrose density gradient (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MurG-Dendra2 is enriched in both the cytoplasmic and IMD membrane fractions.
source: MurG-Dendra2, a peripheral membrane protein, was enriched in both the cytoplasmic and IMD membrane fractions (Figure 1C, top; Figure 1—figure supplements 3A and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: MurG-Dendra2 is a peripheral membrane protein.
source: MurG-Dendra2, a peripheral membrane protein, was enriched in both the cytoplasmic and IMD membrane fractions (Figure 1C, top; Figure 1—figure supplements 3A and 4).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the nature of MurG.

claim: In intact cells, polar enrichment of MurG-Dendra2 is coincident with that of the IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2.
source: In intact cells, polar enrichment of MurG-Dendra2 was coincident with that of the IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Enzymes from the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and shape, elongation, division, and sporulation (SEDS) families integrate the disaccharide-pentapeptide from lipid II into peptidoglycan.
source: Enzymes from the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and shape, elongation, division, and sporulation (SEDS) families integrate the disaccharide-pentapeptide from lipid II into peptidoglycan (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The PM-CW dataset is enriched for all known PBPs.
source: While our proteomics did not detect many polytopic membrane proteins, including SEDS proteins, our PM-CW dataset was enriched for all known PBPs (Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior proteomics data.

claim: Fluorescent derivatives of β-lactam antibiotics, such as Bocillin-FL, bind to PBPs and report transpeptidase-active enzymes.
source: Fluorescent derivatives of β-lactam antibiotics, such as Bocillin-FL, bind to PBPs and report transpeptidase-active enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of Bocillin-FL.

claim: Bocillin-FL-labeled fluorescent proteins are identified in the PM-CW.
source: We incubated subcellular fractions from wild-type M. smegmatis with Bocillin-FL and identified fluorescent proteins in the PM-CW (Figure 1C, bottom; Figure 1—figure supplements 3B and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PonA1 is an essential bifunctional transglycosylase/transpeptidase in M. smegmatis.
source: We focused on characterizing PonA1, an essential bifunctional transglycosylase/transpeptidase in M. smegmatis (Hett et al., 2010; Kieser et al., 2015; Baranowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Depletion of PonA1 results in the loss of the higher molecular band in Bocillin-FL labeling.
source: Depletion of PonA1 (Hett et al., 2010) resulted in the loss of the higher molecular band (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), confirming this protein is present and active in the PM-CW (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: PonA1 is present and active in the PM-CW.
source: Depletion of PonA1 (Hett et al., 2010) resulted in the loss of the higher molecular band (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), confirming this protein is present and active in the PM-CW (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: PonA1-mRFP is a functional fusion protein.
source: We next expressed a functional PonA1-mRFP fusion in M. smegmatis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Kieser et al., 2015; Baranowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PonA1-mRFP is active in the PM-CW.
source: Although we detected potential breakdown products of the fusion protein by anti-RFP immunoblot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we found that it, like native PonA1, was active in the PM-CW and distributed along the sidewall in a manner similar to the functional PM-CW marker PimE-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: PonA1-mRFP distributes along the sidewall in a manner similar to the functional PM-CW marker PimE-GFP.
source: Although we detected potential breakdown products of the fusion protein by anti-RFP immunoblot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we found that it, like native PonA1, was active in the PM-CW and distributed along the sidewall in a manner similar to the functional PM-CW marker PimE-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: MurG and PonA1 have different subcellular localization.
source: Coexpression of MurG-Dendra2 and PonA1-mRFP confirmed that the proteins have different subcellular localization (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MurG and PonA1 occupy membrane compartments that are biochemically and likely spatially distinct.
source: Together, our data show that MurG and PonA1 occupy membrane compartments that are biochemically and likely spatially distinct.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from fractionation and microscopy studies.

claim: The IMD is the site of lipid II synthesis.
source: The association of MurG with the IMD and of PonA1 with the PM-CW implies that the IMD is the site of lipid II synthesis, while the PM-CW is where peptidoglycan assembly takes place.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data of MurG and PonA1.

claim: The PM-CW is where peptidoglycan assembly takes place.
source: The association of MurG with the IMD and of PonA1 with the PM-CW implies that the IMD is the site of lipid II synthesis, while the PM-CW is where peptidoglycan assembly takes place.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data of MurG and PonA1.

claim: Biotinylated molecules are detected in both the IMD and PM-CW in wild-type cells.
source: In wild-type cells, we detected biotinylated molecules in both the IMD and PM-CW (Figure 2C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The labeled species comprise precursors in both the inner and outer leaflets of the plasma membrane.
source: We hypothesized that the labeled species comprise precursors in both the inner and outer leaflets of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Depletion of MurJ results in accumulation of biotinylated precursors.
source: We and others have shown that depletion of MurJ results in accumulation of biotinylated precursors (García-Heredia et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Precursors accumulate in the IMD upon MurJ depletion.
source: By performing the d-amino acid exchange reaction on membrane fractions obtained from MurJ-depleted M. smegmatis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), we found that precursors accumulate in the IMD (Figure 2C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lipid II is made in the IMD and transferred to the PM-CW in a MurJ-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that lipid II is made in the IMD and transferred to the PM-CW in a MurJ-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from MurJ depletion experiments.

claim: Lipid II incorporation into the cell wall is laterally segregated from its synthesis.
source: Based on our biochemical data, we hypothesized that lipid II incorporation into the cell wall is laterally segregated from its synthesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the biochemical data.

claim: Alkynyl and azido d-amino acid dipeptides incorporate into lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors in M. smegmatis.
source: We previously showed that alkynyl and azido d-amino acid dipeptides (Liechti et al., 2014) incorporate into lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors in M. smegmatis (García-Heredia et al., 2018) and that metabolic labeling with alkynyl dipeptide (alkDADA or EDA-DA, Liechti et al., 2014) is most intense in regions adjacent to the IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2 (Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Metabolic labeling with alkDADA is most intense in regions adjacent to the IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2.
source: We previously showed that alkynyl and azido d-amino acid dipeptides (Liechti et al., 2014) incorporate into lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors in M. smegmatis (García-Heredia et al., 2018) and that metabolic labeling with alkynyl dipeptide (alkDADA or EDA-DA, Liechti et al., 2014) is most intense in regions adjacent to the IMD marker mCherry-GlfT2 (Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Picolyl azide-Cy3 has poor membrane permeability.
source: To distinguish extracellular alkynes present in periplasmic lipid II and newly polymerized cell wall from alkynes originating from cytoplasmic lipid II, we selected picolyl azide-Cy3 as our label because of its poor membrane permeability (Figure 2B, Yang and Hinner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Nascent peptidoglycan deposition occurs at the polar tip, whereas MurG-Dendra2 is proximal to this site.
source: Using this optimized protocol, we observed nascent peptidoglycan deposition at the polar tip, whereas MurG-Dendra2 was proximal to this site (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Lipid II synthesis is laterally partitioned from the subsequent steps of peptidoglycan assembly.
source: Our data suggest that lipid II synthesis is laterally partitioned from the subsequent steps of peptidoglycan assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from microscopy and biochemical assays.

claim: MurJ depletion reduced and delocalized alkDADA-derived fluorescence.
source: MurJ depletion reduced and delocalized alkDADA-derived fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), consistent with a gatekeeper role for the flippase in both lateral membrane compartmentalization and flipping across the inner membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: MurJ has a gatekeeper role in both lateral membrane compartmentalization and flipping across the inner membrane.
source: MurJ depletion reduced and delocalized alkDADA-derived fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), consistent with a gatekeeper role for the flippase in both lateral membrane compartmentalization and flipping across the inner membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Benzyl alcohol preferentially inserts into disordered membrane regions in vitro.
source: We perturbed the membrane with benzyl alcohol, a compound that preferentially inserts into disordered membrane regions in vitro (Muddana et al., 2012) and has been used to fluidize membranes from mammalian and bacterial cells (Friedlander et al., 1987; Ingram, 1976; Konopásek et al., 2000; Nagy et al., 2007; Strahl et al., 2014; Zielińska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Benzyl alcohol has been used to fluidize membranes from mammalian and bacterial cells.
source: We perturbed the membrane with benzyl alcohol, a compound that preferentially inserts into disordered membrane regions in vitro (Muddana et al., 2012) and has been used to fluidize membranes from mammalian and bacterial cells (Friedlander et al., 1987; Ingram, 1976; Konopásek et al., 2000; Nagy et al., 2007; Strahl et al., 2014; Zielińska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Benzyl alcohol disrupts RIFs in B. subtilis.
source: In B. subtilis, benzyl alcohol disrupts RIFs (Müller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Benzyl alcohol reduced the cellular material associated with the IMD in M. smegmatis.
source: In M. smegmatis, we found that benzyl alcohol reduced the cellular material associated with the IMD (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and altered the distribution of FM4-64, a non-specific lipophilic dye (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and of plasma membrane glycolipids (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Benzyl alcohol altered the distribution of FM4-64 in M. smegmatis.
source: In M. smegmatis, we found that benzyl alcohol reduced the cellular material associated with the IMD (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and altered the distribution of FM4-64, a non-specific lipophilic dye (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and of plasma membrane glycolipids (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Benzyl alcohol altered the distribution of plasma membrane glycolipids in M. smegmatis.
source: In M. smegmatis, we found that benzyl alcohol reduced the cellular material associated with the IMD (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and altered the distribution of FM4-64, a non-specific lipophilic dye (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and of plasma membrane glycolipids (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Benzyl alcohol did not alter labeling by N-AlkTMM or O-AlkTMM.
source: However, the fluidizer did not alter labeling by N-AlkTMM or O-AlkTMM (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), probes that, respectively, mark the noncovalent and covalent lipids of the outer 'myco' membrane (Foley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: N-AlkTMM and O-AlkTMM mark the noncovalent and covalent lipids of the outer 'myco' membrane, respectively.
source: However, the fluidizer did not alter labeling by N-AlkTMM or O-AlkTMM (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), probes that, respectively, mark the noncovalent and covalent lipids of the outer 'myco' membrane (Foley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Benzyl alcohol primarily affects the plasma membrane in M. smegmatis.
source: These observations suggest that benzyl alcohol primarily affects the plasma membrane in M. smegmatis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: MurG-Dendra2 was less enriched in the IMD fraction following benzyl alcohol treatment.
source: MurG-Dendra2 was also less enriched in the IMD fraction following benzyl alcohol treatment (Figure 1C, top; Figure 1—figure supplements 3E and 4) and, in live cells, at the poles (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2A.

claim: MurG-Dendra2 was less enriched at the poles in live cells following benzyl alcohol treatment.
source: MurG-Dendra2 was also less enriched in the IMD fraction following benzyl alcohol treatment (Figure 1C, top; Figure 1—figure supplements 3E and 4) and, in live cells, at the poles (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Benzyl alcohol produced subtle changes in the subcellular distribution of active PBPs.
source: By contrast, benzyl alcohol produced subtle changes in the subcellular distribution of active PBPs (Figure 1C, bottom; Figure 1—figure supplements 3D and 4), although PonA1 shifted toward the poles in live cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PonA1 shifted toward the poles in live cells following benzyl alcohol treatment.
source: By contrast, benzyl alcohol produced subtle changes in the subcellular distribution of active PBPs (Figure 1C, bottom; Figure 1—figure supplements 3D and 4), although PonA1 shifted toward the poles in live cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Disruption of plasma membrane architecture was accompanied by dampening and delocalization of peptidoglycan assembly.
source: Disruption of plasma membrane architecture was accompanied by dampening and delocalization of peptidoglycan assembly (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5) as well as a reduction in lipid precursor synthesis (Figure 3C) and halt in polar elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: Disruption of plasma membrane architecture was accompanied by a reduction in lipid precursor synthesis.
source: Disruption of plasma membrane architecture was accompanied by dampening and delocalization of peptidoglycan assembly (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5) as well as a reduction in lipid precursor synthesis (Figure 3C) and halt in polar elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Disruption of plasma membrane architecture was accompanied by a halt in polar elongation.
source: Disruption of plasma membrane architecture was accompanied by dampening and delocalization of peptidoglycan assembly (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5) as well as a reduction in lipid precursor synthesis (Figure 3C) and halt in polar elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The effects of benzyl alcohol were reversible.
source: The effects of benzyl alcohol were reversible, as indicated by colony-forming units and prompt recovery of peptidoglycan synthesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Dibucaine preferentially disrupts ordered membrane regions in vitro.
source: Dibucaine, a compound that preferentially disrupts ordered membrane regions in vitro (Kinoshita et al., 2019) and can fluidize membranes from eukaryotic cells (Kim et al., 1997), also delocalized IMD-resident proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) and delocalized and reduced peptidoglycan synthesis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Dibucaine can fluidize membranes from eukaryotic cells.
source: Dibucaine, a compound that preferentially disrupts ordered membrane regions in vitro (Kinoshita et al., 2019) and can fluidize membranes from eukaryotic cells (Kim et al., 1997), also delocalized IMD-resident proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) and delocalized and reduced peptidoglycan synthesis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Dibucaine delocalized IMD-resident proteins.
source: Dibucaine, a compound that preferentially disrupts ordered membrane regions in vitro (Kinoshita et al., 2019) and can fluidize membranes from eukaryotic cells (Kim et al., 1997), also delocalized IMD-resident proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) and delocalized and reduced peptidoglycan synthesis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Dibucaine delocalized and reduced peptidoglycan synthesis.
source: Dibucaine, a compound that preferentially disrupts ordered membrane regions in vitro (Kinoshita et al., 2019) and can fluidize membranes from eukaryotic cells (Kim et al., 1997), also delocalized IMD-resident proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) and delocalized and reduced peptidoglycan synthesis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Membrane architecture contributes to peptidoglycan synthesis and cell growth in M. smegmatis.
source: Our data suggest that membrane architecture contributes to peptidoglycan synthesis and cell growth in M. smegmatis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from membrane perturbation experiments.

claim: Benzyl alcohol decreases peptidoglycan precursor accumulation.
source: While we cannot rule out pleiotropic effects of chemical fluidizers on membrane potential or membrane protein activity, we note that benzyl alcohol decreases peptidoglycan precursor accumulation (Figure 3C), rather than increasing it as occurs with protonophore treatment (Rubino et al., 2018) or MurJ depletion (Figure 2C; García-Heredia et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017); MurG and PonA1 are retained in the membrane upon benzyl alcohol treatment (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4); and at least a subset of membrane-bound PBPs remain competent for Bocillin-FL binding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Protonophore treatment increases peptidoglycan precursor accumulation.
source: While we cannot rule out pleiotropic effects of chemical fluidizers on membrane potential or membrane protein activity, we note that benzyl alcohol decreases peptidoglycan precursor accumulation (Figure 3C), rather than increasing it as occurs with protonophore treatment (Rubino et al., 2018) or MurJ depletion (Figure 2C; García-Heredia et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017); MurG and PonA1 are retained in the membrane upon benzyl alcohol treatment (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4); and at least a subset of membrane-bound PBPs remain competent for Bocillin-FL binding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: MurG and PonA1 are retained in the membrane upon benzyl alcohol treatment.
source: While we cannot rule out pleiotropic effects of chemical fluidizers on membrane potential or membrane protein activity, we note that benzyl alcohol decreases peptidoglycan precursor accumulation (Figure 3C), rather than increasing it as occurs with protonophore treatment (Rubino et al., 2018) or MurJ depletion (Figure 2C; García-Heredia et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017); MurG and PonA1 are retained in the membrane upon benzyl alcohol treatment (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4); and at least a subset of membrane-bound PBPs remain competent for Bocillin-FL binding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: At least a subset of membrane-bound PBPs remain competent for Bocillin-FL binding upon benzyl alcohol treatment.
source: While we cannot rule out pleiotropic effects of chemical fluidizers on membrane potential or membrane protein activity, we note that benzyl alcohol decreases peptidoglycan precursor accumulation (Figure 3C), rather than increasing it as occurs with protonophore treatment (Rubino et al., 2018) or MurJ depletion (Figure 2C; García-Heredia et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017); MurG and PonA1 are retained in the membrane upon benzyl alcohol treatment (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4); and at least a subset of membrane-bound PBPs remain competent for Bocillin-FL binding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Benzyl alcohol and dibucaine delocalize nascent peptidoglycan from the poles to the sidewall.
